name: World Stats
author: yakuda
description: Four things your chatbox line usually wants and VRChat does not send over OSC. Instance info: how many players are around you, the world name and the access type, read from VRChat's output_log - Steam/Proton prefix on Linux, AppData\\LocalLow on Windows - with no extra tools. Two session counters: how long you have been in the current instance and how long you have been in VR this session, both taken from the log's own timestamps so they keep counting when the chatbox is restarted mid-session. A clock that stands on its own: it has no connection to the log watcher and keeps running when VRChat is closed, with an optional date, weekday and a second time zone for friends abroad. Your headset battery, read either over adb from the headset itself - Quest, Pico, Vive Focus, no matter whether you stream with WiVRn, ALVR or nothing at all - over the running OpenXR runtime through libmonado, or over SteamVR/OpenVR. And your frame rate: on Linux from a small Vulkan layer the plugin builds and loads into the game itself, so nothing else has to be installed - MangoHud's log still works as an alternative. On Windows from RTSS, because VRChat renders D3D11 there and a Vulkan layer would never see it. Every part can be used without the others.
summary: Players, world and instance type, a standalone clock, headset/controller battery, and your frame rate.

placeholders.fps_raw: frames per second, the bare number
placeholders.fps_source: which backend answered - layer / MangoHud / RTSS
placeholders.player_in_world: number of players in the instance
placeholders.world_time: how long you have been in this instance
placeholders.vr_time: how long VRChat has been running
placeholders.realtime_alt: the clock in a second time zone

settings.label: Player icon
settings.hint: Prefix in front of the player count, empty for none

settings.label: World name length
settings.hint: Longer names are cut off - the chatbox has limited space

settings.label: Frame rate
settings.hint: Frames per second only exist inside the process drawing them - nothing in the operating system knows how fast a game is rendering, so something has to be loaded into the game. On Linux this plugin ships a small Vulkan layer that does exactly that. On Windows it reads RTSS, because VRChat renders D3D11 there and a Vulkan layer would never see it.

items.label: Frame rate  –  {fps}
items.hint: On Linux this also arms the Vulkan layer: switching it on writes a file into ~/.local/share/vulkan/implicit_layer.d, switching it off deletes it again. Nothing keeps running while this is off. A game that was already open when you tick this has to be restarted - the loader reads that folder once, when the game starts.

items.label: Status
items.hint: Written by the plugin: which backend answered, which process it is reading, and what it reads.

items.label: Check it now
items.hint: Re-reads everything and says which game, if any, is currently reporting a frame rate.

items.label: Where to read it from
items.hint: Auto tries the built-in layer first and falls back to a MangoHud log, so anyone who already has MangoHud working keeps working. Windows ignores this - RTSS is the only source there.

items.label: Prefer this process
items.hint: Part of the executable name. Without it a browser playing a video, or the desktop compositor, can outrank the game on an idle machine. Leave it empty to always take whatever is drawing the most.

items.label: FPS icon
items.hint: In front of the number, empty for none

items.label: Write "FPS" after the number
items.hint: Off saves four characters, which the chatbox can use for something else.

items.label: Frame time too  –  {frametime}
items.hint: Milliseconds per frame. The number that actually tells you whether a session is smooth - 11.1 ms is 90 fps, and a jump to 22 ms is a dropped frame you can feel.

items.label: Only show below
items.hint: Leave at 0 to always show it. Set it and the placeholder stays empty while the frame rate is fine - for people who only want the line to appear when something is wrong.

items.label: Vulkan layer  –  Linux
items.hint: About 500 lines of C in the plugin's layer/ folder whose entire job is to count calls to vkQueuePresentKHR and publish the rate in shared memory. It draws nothing, adds no overlay, enables no extension and allocates nothing per frame - a frame counter that hitches the frame rate it is measuring would be worse than useless. VRChat under Proton renders through DXVK, which is Vulkan, so it is covered like a native Vulkan title. OpenGL-only games are not; MangoHud has the same blind spot for the same reason. DREAMFPS_DISABLE=1 switches it off for a single process without touching the settings.

items.label: Build the layer
items.hint: Compiles layer/dreamfps_layer.c with the compiler already on your system. Needs gcc, make and the Vulkan headers - Arch: base-devel vulkan-headers, Fedora: gcc make vulkan-headers, Debian: build-essential libvulkan-dev. The plugin ships the source rather than a prebuilt binary on purpose: this thing loads into every Vulkan application you run, and that should be something you could have read first.

items.label: MangoHud log  –  Linux
items.hint: The older route, kept because plenty of people already have it set up. Switch CSV logging on in MangoHud or GOverlay, then point this at the folder it writes to.

items.label: Log folder
items.hint: Where MangoHud writes its .csv logs. Only the newest one is read, and only its last few lines.

items.label: Find it for me
items.hint: Reads output_folder out of your MangoHud configs - including the per-game ones and the ones GOverlay writes, which is how most people set logging up without ever seeing the path - and falls back to the usual folders. A folder holding VRChat logs wins over one holding somebody else's benchmark.

items.label: RTSS  –  Windows
items.hint: RivaTuner Statistics Server ships with MSI Afterburner and is what nearly every Windows overlay already uses. The plugin only reads the shared memory block RTSS publishes - no injection of its own, no admin rights, nothing that anti-cheat has to have an opinion about. Install it, leave it running, and the frame rate appears.

settings.label: Session time
settings.hint: Both counters are read out of the log's own timestamps, not measured with a stopwatch started here - restart the chatbox in the middle of a session and they carry on where they were instead of jumping back to zero.

items.label: Time in this world  –  {world_time}
items.hint: Counts from the moment you joined the instance and resets when you leave. Empty while you are not in a world.

items.label: Time in VR  –  {vr_time}
items.hint: The long one: how far into this session you are, across every world you have been through.

items.label: Counted from
items.hint: VRChat is the honest answer to "how long have I been in VR" - it is the first line of the current log file, so it survives an app restart. The other one is a plain stopwatch and only matches your session if you started the chatbox first.

items.label: Only show after
items.hint: Below this the placeholder stays empty instead of announcing that you have been here for zero minutes. Set it to 0 to always show it.

settings.label: Clock
settings.hint: Completely independent of the two rows above. The clock needs no log file, no VRChat and no headset - switch players and world name off and this keeps running on its own.

items.label: Clock format
items.hint: strftime, e.g. %H:%M (21:45) or %I:%M %p (09:45 PM)

items.label: Time zone
items.hint: An IANA name like Europe/Berlin or America/New_York. Leave empty to follow the system clock. On Windows this needs the tzdata package; if a zone cannot be loaded the plugin falls back to local time and says so in the log.

items.label: Date format
items.hint: strftime again, e.g. %d.%m. (24.08.) or %b %d (Aug 24)

items.label: Second time zone  –  {realtime_alt}
items.hint: A second clock next to yours - handy when the people you talk to are in another country.

items.label: Second zone
items.hint: IANA name, same as above

items.label: Second zone prefix
items.hint: Written in front of the second clock, empty for none

settings.label: Headset battery
settings.hint: Also independent of the rest - it works outside a world and outside VRChat.

items.label: Battery  –  {hmd_battery}
items.hint: Off means off: no adb process and no OpenVR session are kept alive while this is unchecked.

items.label: Status
items.hint: Written by the plugin: which backend answered, which headset, and what it reads.

items.label: Read the battery now
items.hint: Skips the wait for the next poll and answers right here.

items.label: Where to read it from
items.hint: Auto asks the OpenXR runtime first, then SteamVR, then adb. Pin it to one to skip the probes for the others.

items.label: Read every
items.hint: A battery moves by one percent every few minutes, so there is nothing to gain below a minute - and adb costs a process each time.

items.label: Only show below
items.hint: Leave at 100 to always show it. Lower it and the placeholder stays empty while the headset is still full - the chatbox gets those characters back for something worth saying.

items.label: Controllers and trackers too  –  {controller_battery} {tracker_battery}
items.hint: WiVRn/Monado and SteamVR only – Android knows nothing about the controllers, so this stays empty on the adb backend.

items.label: Icons
items.hint: The emoji in front of each number. Leave one empty to drop the prefix for that placeholder.

items.label: Charging icon
items.hint: Replaces the icon above while the headset is on the cable, empty to keep the same icon either way

items.label: Tracker icon
items.hint: The tracker placeholder shows the emptiest tracker, not all of them - that is the one you want to know about.

items.label: WiVRn / Monado
items.hint: Reads libmonado, the same library WayVR and Monado's own tools use. Nothing to install and nothing to configure: the library is found through the active_runtime.json of whichever runtime is currently active. It answers only while a session is running, and it never starts one. The library is loaded in a short-lived helper process, not in the app - if it crashes or hangs, this backend goes quiet for 30 seconds and the chatbox carries on.

items.label: libmonado
items.hint: Written by the plugin: where libmonado was found, or why it was not.

items.label: adb  –  standalone headsets
items.hint: Quest, Pico, Vive Focus and friends. The headset has to be attached over USB or over the network, and you have to accept the USB debugging prompt inside the headset once.

items.label: adb binary
items.hint: Only needed when adb is not on PATH. On Arch it comes with android-tools, on Fedora with android-tools, on Debian with adb.

items.label: Device serial
items.hint: Only matters with more than one device attached - a phone counts. The panel below lists the serials.

items.label: Wireless address
items.hint: For reading the battery over WiFi instead of the cable. Enable wireless debugging in the headset first; port 5555 is assumed when you leave it off.

items.label: Connect to that address
items.hint: Runs adb connect once. It stays connected until the headset reboots or leaves the network.

items.label: SteamVR
items.hint: Reads SteamVR's own device list. The plugin attaches as a background application, which never starts SteamVR by itself - while SteamVR is closed this backend simply reports nothing.

items.label: Install the openvr package
items.hint: pip install openvr into the interpreter the app runs on. Needs an app restart afterwards. Skip this entirely if you only use the adb backend.

settings.label: VRChat log folder
settings.hint: Leave empty for auto-detect - Steam/Proton prefix on Linux, AppData\\LocalLow on Windows. Only the players/world rows use this; clock and battery do not touch it.
